specPoints.text: understand how a chromatogram provides information about the composition of a mixture
understand how to use the calculation of Rf values to identify the components of a mixture

primer.text: You already know from Separation Techniques how paper chromatography separates the components of an ink. This note reads the result: what the spots say about purity and composition, and how Rf values put numbers on each component so unknowns can be named.

lessons.title: Reading the Spots
lessons.opening: A chromatogram is the finished paper after a run, and it reads like a list of ingredients. One spot means a pure substance; several spots mean a mixture, because each component travels to its own height. Run known compounds alongside as reference spots, and any unknown whose dots line up horizontally with a reference is named.
keyPoints: A pure substance produces one spot on a chromatogram; an impure sample produces more than one.
A mixture separates on the paper, showing each of its components as a separate spot.
Identical substances produce identical chromatograms under the same conditions.
A known compound run as a reference spot helps match and identify unknown spots.
The brown ink's three dots line up horizontally with red, yellow and blue, so the ink contains all three.
Exam chromatograms are black and white, so matching is done by horizontal alignment of dots.

low.restatement: Count the spots: one means pure, several means a mixture with every component showing its own spot. Dots at the same height came from the same substance, so a reference chemical settles what an unknown contains.
low.analogy: It is like footprints marked at different heights on a wall chart: everyone who reached the same line took the same climb.
low.examPointer: Spot counts decide pure versus impure; horizontal alignment decides which substance is which.

medium.restatement: Each component of a mixture travels to its own characteristic height, so the finished chromatogram displays the components as separate spots — one spot for a pure substance, several for a mixture. A known compound run alongside acts as a reference: any unknown spot sitting level with it belongs to that substance, which is how exam chromatograms identify components without colour.
medium.analogy: Athletes on a climbing wall reach different holds; the height each one ends at is their signature, and matching heights match the climbers.
medium.examPointer: In black-and-white papers, match dots by level lines, never by shade.

check.stem: A chromatogram shows four separate spots stacked at different heights. What was applied to the baseline?

options.text: A mixture — each component shows as its own spot
options.explanation: Several spots mean several substances travelled, which is a mixture.

options.text: A pure substance — one chemical always gives four dots
options.explanation: A pure substance gives exactly one spot.

options.text: An element — dots prove atomic simplicity
options.explanation: Chromatography says nothing about elements versus compounds, only how many substances are present.

options.text: A compound with four bonds
options.explanation: Spot count counts substances, not bonds.

check.stem: Brown ink is run beside red, yellow and blue inks. The brown leaves three dots, each level with one of the others. What follows?

options.text: The brown ink is a mixture of the red, yellow and blue inks
options.explanation: Level dots mean identical substances, and three of them make up the brown.

options.text: The brown ink is pure, since its dots are level
options.explanation: Three dots is three substances — the very picture of a mixture here.

options.text: The inks reacted to make brown during the run
options.explanation: No reaction occurs; the brown was mixed before it reached the paper.

options.text: The chromatogram is faulty and should be repeated
options.explanation: The result is exactly what a mixture of three dyes looks like.

check.stem: Why is a reference spot of a known compound included on the same paper?

options.text: So unknown spots that line up with it can be identified by matching
options.explanation: A level line between reference and unknown means the same substance.

options.text: To make the chromatogram look complete
options.explanation: The reference has a working role, not a decorative one.

options.text: To use up spare space on the paper
options.explanation: Space is not the concern; identification is.

options.text: Because every valid chromatogram must contain four spots
options.explanation: There is no spot-count rule; references exist to match against.

check.stem: Two samples give chromatograms whose spots sit at exactly the same heights. What can be concluded?

options.text: The samples are the same substance
options.explanation: Identical substances produce identical chromatograms.

options.text: One sample is purer than the other
options.explanation: Same spots, same purity picture; nothing distinguishes them.

options.text: The solvent was different for each
options.explanation: A different solvent would shift the heights.

options.text: The samples are mixtures of the same colour
options.explanation: Height matching identifies substances regardless of colour.

check.stem: An exam prints a chromatogram in black and white. How do you tell whether a mixture contains a given known sample?

options.text: Check whether the mixture's dots line up horizontally with the known's dots
options.explanation: In black and white, level alignment is the only reliable match.

options.text: Compare the darkness of the spots
options.explanation: Shade depends on quantity and printing, not identity.

options.text: Count which sample has more dots overall
options.explanation: Counts say pure versus mixture, not which substances are shared.

options.text: Measure which spots are widest
options.explanation: Spot width is not the identification criterion.

lessons.title: Rf Values
lessons.opening: Every substance has a retention factor: the distance it moves up the paper divided by the distance the solvent front moves. The value is a ratio with no units, always less than one, and constant for that substance in that solvent — change the solvent and the value changes with it. Compare measured values against known ones and unknown components can be named.
keyPoints: Rf equals the distance moved by the substance divided by the distance moved by the solvent.
The value is a ratio, carries no units, and always stays below one.
A compound keeps the same Rf in the same solvent, but a new solvent changes it.
Measured Rf values compared with tables of known values identify the components of a mixture.
Measure both distances from the baseline to the centre of each dot or front.
Strict mark schemes reward careful ruler work on both distances.

low.restatement: Divide how far the spot climbed by how far the solvent climbed: that number is Rf. It has no units, never reaches one, and repeats exactly while the solvent stays the same. Comparing the value with recorded tables names the substance, provided the same solvent was used.
low.analogy: If the solvent front runs a full race and the substance completes half of it, the substance's score is 0.5.
low.examPointer: Anchor both measurements at the baseline and read to the centre of the dot.

medium.restatement: The retention factor is computed as the distance moved by the substance over the distance moved by the solvent front, both measured from the pencil baseline. Being a ratio it carries no units and must stay below one, since the substance can never outrun the solvent that carries it; a fresh solvent re-sets the value, so tables of known values apply only under matching conditions.
medium.analogy: Treat the solvent front as the full length of a swimming pool and the spot as one swimmer's lap: the fraction completed is the swimmer's score, whatever the pool's size.
medium.examPointer: Change the solvent and every Rf changes with it — state the solvent when quoting values.

check.stem: What is the Rf value of a substance?

options.text: Distance moved by the substance divided by distance moved by the solvent
options.explanation: Both distances are measured from the baseline.

options.text: Distance moved by the solvent divided by distance moved by the substance
options.explanation: That inverts the ratio and pushes values above one.

options.text: The time the substance takes to climb the paper
options.explanation: Rf is about distances, not times.

options.text: The mass of substance dissolved in the solvent
options.explanation: No mass enters the calculation.

check.stem: Why must every Rf value be smaller than one?

options.text: The substance cannot travel further than the solvent that carries it
options.explanation: The solvent front sets the maximum distance, so the ratio stays below one.

options.text: Values above one are simply rounded down
options.explanation: The bound is physical, not a rounding convention.

options.text: Because Rf is measured in centimetres
options.explanation: Rf has no units at all.

options.text: One is the maximum solubility allowed
options.explanation: Solubility does not cap the ratio; the geometry of the run does.

check.stem: A student measures Rf = 0.4 in one solvent, then repeats the run in a different solvent. What happens?

options.text: The Rf value can change, because it depends on the solvent used
options.explanation: The value is constant only for a given substance in a given solvent.

options.text: The Rf stays 0.4 in every solvent
options.explanation: Changing the solvent changes the value.

options.text: Rf doubles when the solvent changes
options.explanation: There is no fixed scaling between solvents.

options.text: Rf becomes meaningless after the first run
options.explanation: Each run gives a valid value for its own solvent.

check.stem: Where exactly are the two distances for an Rf calculation measured from and to?

options.text: From the baseline to the centre of the dot, and to the solvent front
options.explanation: Baseline to centre for the substance; baseline to front for the solvent.

options.text: From the top of the paper down to the dots
options.explanation: Both distances run upward from the same baseline.

options.text: From dot edge to dot edge
options.explanation: Centres, not edges, are the marked convention.

options.text: From the solvent container to the pencil line
options.explanation: The container plays no part; the paper's baseline is the anchor.

check.stem: Why can Rf values identify an unknown component of a mixture?

options.text: Because a substance's Rf under the same conditions matches a known value in the tables
options.explanation: Same substance, same solvent, same value — the match names the component.

options.text: Because every substance has a unique Rf across all solvents
options.explanation: The value is unique only within a fixed solvent; the table must match conditions.

options.text: Because higher spots always mean bigger molecules
options.explanation: Travel reflects solubility in the solvent, not molecular size rules of thumb.

options.text: Because the solvent records its own fingerprint
options.explanation: The identification reads the spots, not the solvent.

glossary.definition: Taking a mixture apart into its components by physical means.
The visual output of a chromatography run: the paper with its separated spots after the run.
A spot of a known compound run alongside unknowns so spots can be matched.
A substance that gives a single spot on a chromatogram.
The pencil starting line on chromatography paper where samples are spotted.
The ratio of the distance moved by a substance to the distance moved by the solvent.
The liquid that travels up the paper and carries the substances with it.

workedExample.prompt: A student runs a chromatogram and measures the distance moved by the substance as 3 units and the distance moved by the solvent as 6 units. Calculate the Rf value of the substance.
steps: Distance moved by the substance, measured baseline to centre: 3 on the printed scale.
Distance moved by the solvent, measured baseline to front: 6 on the same scale.
Rf value: 3 / 6 = 0.5, a ratio with no units.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Rf = 0.5 for that substance in that solvent.
